source_note: Richard Szeliski, Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications, Springer, 2010 (first edition). The local file is the author's own electronic draft: its title page reads 'September 3, 2010 draft' and 'c 2010 Springer', marked for non-commercial personal use and pointing to szeliski.org/Book. The library filename carries a 2022 year tag (Szeliski-2022-ComputerVisionAlgorithmsAndApplications-Draft.pdf, bucket books-d-models); the file's content is the 2010 draft of the same work, so the tasking description '2010 draft text' is correct in substance and the 2022 filename year is a cataloging artifact. File size 23210750 bytes; gatekeeper scan digest (sha256 over str(size) plus full file bytes) 2c0ae9d774fc0d420db8521511a6d1e139dcc3e622130ad65f4da010005f6a45; book_id is its first 16 hex characters. Extracted text is 2530781 bytes over 38872 lines, clean born-digital text; displayed equations are partly glyph-corrupted in the extraction, so every verbatim quote was drawn from clean prose passages and proven contiguous in the text file, and each LaTeX field transcribes the numbered equation printed at the cited location. Motif-lane extraction (MOTIF-TIERB-DRAIN-01) of the same work for sync-cloud reconciliation.

primitives.name: Vision is an inverse problem: recover unknowns from insufficient information using physics-based and probabilistic models
primitives.verbatim_quote:
In part, it is because
vision is an inverse problem, in which we seek to recover some unknowns given insufficient
information to fully specify the solution.
assumptions: The forward imaging process loses information (projection, sampling, noise), so the inverse is underdetermined
Physics-based and probabilistic priors are available to disambiguate candidate solutions
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails as a framing when the forward model is unknown or the priors are wrong; then the recovered unknowns are artifacts of the model, not the scene

layer2.mapping: The engine treats every signal as an observation generated by a hidden state through a lossy forward process; inference must therefore combine the observation with explicit priors and report the ambiguity that remains instead of a single forced answer
layer2.telemetry: observation counts per hidden variable, prior strengths, residual ambiguity after conditioning

primitives.name: Homogeneous coordinates: 2D points as scale-equivalent vectors in projective space P2, with ideal points at w=0
primitives.verbatim_quote:
2D points can also be represented using homogeneous coordinates, x̃ = (x̃, ỹ, w̃) ∈ P 2 ,
where vectors that differ only by scale are considered to be equivalent.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\tilde{x}: homogeneous 2D point, defined up to nonzero scale
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\tilde{w}: homogeneous scale component; w=0 marks a point at infinity
symbol_and_unit_ledger.P2: 2D projective space, R3 minus the origin

assumptions: Scale equivalence: vectors differing only by a nonzero scalar denote the same point
Conversion back to inhomogeneous coordinates divides through by the last element
primitives.breakdown_regime: Points with last element 0 are ideal points (points at infinity) and have no inhomogeneous equivalent; naive division by w explodes near w=0

layer2.mapping: Representing quantities up to scale lets the engine carry ratio-scale evidence (relative strengths) through linear algebra without premature normalization, and treats degenerate zero-scale cases as a distinct regime rather than a numeric blowup
layer2.telemetry: scale factors carried per quantity, count of near-zero denominators flagged as degenerate

primitives.name: Perspective projection divides by depth (x/z, y/z), so a single image cannot recover point distance
primitives.verbatim_quote:
Thus, after projection, it is not possible to recover the
distance of the 3D point from the image, which makes sense for a 2D imaging sensor.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.p = (x, y, z): 3D point in camera coordinates, length units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.z: depth along the optical axis, length units, z > 0 in front of the camera
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\bar{x}: projected inhomogeneous image point, dimensionless ratios

assumptions: Pinhole (central) projection through a single center of projection
Point lies in front of the camera (positive depth)
primitives.breakdown_regime: Depth is unrecoverable from one view; points at z near 0 project unstably and points behind the camera flip sign

layer2.mapping: A single observation channel that divides out a latent variable mirrors any one-number summary of a multi-factor situation: the engine must treat the divided-out factor as unobserved and recover it only from additional independent views
layer2.telemetry: number of independent views per quantity, depth-like latent variables flagged unobserved from a single channel

primitives.name: Projective transformation (homography): an arbitrary 3x3 homogeneous matrix maps points between planes, defined up to scale
primitives.verbatim_quote:
This transformation, also known as a perspective transform or homography,
operates on homogeneous coordinates,

symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\tilde{H}: arbitrary 3x3 homography matrix, defined up to a nonzero scale factor (8 degrees of freedom)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\tilde{x}, \\tilde{x}': homogeneous 2D points before and after the transform

assumptions: The scene points lie on a plane, or the camera motion is a pure rotation, for a single homography to relate two views exactly
Correspondences are available to estimate the 8 degrees of freedom
primitives.breakdown_regime: Non-planar scenes with general camera translation violate a single global homography; parallax appears as systematic residual

layer2.mapping: Plane-induced warping is the template for mapping evidence between two frames of reference with a single linear operator estimated from correspondences; the engine uses the same pattern whenever two representations of the same situation must be registered before comparison
layer2.telemetry: correspondence counts, registration residuals, parallax-like systematic misfit

primitives.name: Lambertian (diffuse) reflection: constant BRDF, scattered uniformly in all directions; shading varies with the light incidence angle
primitives.verbatim_quote:
The diffuse component (also known as Lambertian or matte reflection) scatters light uni-
formly in all directions and is the phenomenon we most normally associate with shading,

symbol_and_unit_ledger.f_d: diffuse BRDF, per unit wavelength, independent of view and light direction for a Lambertian surface
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\hat{v}_i, \\hat{v}_r: unit incident and reflected direction vectors

assumptions: Surface microstructure scatters light uniformly into the hemisphere
Selective absorption inside the material gives the reflected light its body color
primitives.breakdown_regime: Specular (shiny) materials, retroreflectors, and subsurface-scattering media violate the constant-BRDF assumption; self-shadowing kills the signal at grazing angles

layer2.mapping: A response that depends only on the angle between input direction and surface orientation, not on the observer, is the model for any orientation-dependent but observer-independent signal strength; the engine can factor such responses into an intrinsic albedo-like term and a geometric foreshortening term
layer2.telemetry: incidence angles per observation, estimated intrinsic response after removing geometric falloff

primitives.name: Bayer pattern: green filters on half the sensors, red and blue on the rest; missing colors recovered by demosaicing
primitives.verbatim_quote:
The most commonly used pattern in color cameras today is the Bayer pattern (Bayer
1976), which places green filters over half of the sensors (in a checkerboard pattern), and red
and blue filters over the remaining ones (Figure 2.30).
assumptions: Luminance is carried mostly by green, and human vision is far more sensitive to luminance than chrominance detail, justifying 2x green sampling
Neighboring pixels are correlated enough that missing color values can be interpolated
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fine colored detail at the sampling limit aliases (moiré); interpolation fails at sharp color edges and on saturated pixels

layer2.mapping: Deliberately uneven sampling, dense where the information content is highest and sparse elsewhere with model-based interpolation, is a resource allocation template: the engine samples its most informative channels at full rate and reconstructs the rest under a smoothness prior
layer2.telemetry: sampling rates per channel, interpolation residuals at discontinuities

primitives.name: Convolution and correlation are linear shift-invariant operators obeying superposition and shift invariance
primitives.verbatim_quote:
Both correlation and convolution are linear shift-invariant (LSI) operators, which obey
both the superposition principle (3.5),

symbol_and_unit_ledger.h: filter kernel, the impulse response function
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\ast: convolution operator (kernel offsets sign-reversed relative to correlation)

assumptions: The operator is linear: response to a sum is the sum of responses
The operator is shift-invariant: it behaves the same everywhere in the image
primitives.breakdown_regime: Position-dependent blur, saturation, and any data-dependent weighting break linearity or shift invariance, and the convolution model then misdescribes the system

layer2.mapping: When a processing stage is linear and shift-invariant, its whole behavior is one impulse response and superposition holds; the engine uses this to decide which signal pipelines can be analyzed, cached, and inverted component-wise and which need non-linear treatment
layer2.telemetry: per-stage linearity checks, impulse response estimates, superposition residuals

primitives.name: Fourier transform tabulates magnitude and phase response per frequency; convolution in space is multiplication in frequency
primitives.verbatim_quote:
Fourier transform of two convolved images is the product of their individual Fourier trans-
forms (Section 3.4).
primitives.page: Sections 3.2 and 3.4, printed pp. 113 and 134 (text lines ~5392-5395 and 6299-6303)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.H(\\omega): frequency response of filter h at angular frequency \omega
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\omega: angular frequency, radians per unit length

assumptions: The system is linear shift-invariant, so sinusoids are its eigenfunctions
Signals are treated as periodic or sufficiently padded at the boundaries
primitives.breakdown_regime: Non-linear or spatially varying operators have no single frequency response; finite windows leak energy across frequencies

layer2.mapping: Decomposing a signal into frequency bands separates slow structure from fast fluctuation; the engine applies the same decomposition to time series of evidence so that trend, cycle, and noise are weighed separately instead of being averaged into one number
layer2.telemetry: per-band energy of evidence series, band-limited residuals

primitives.name: Burt and Adelson Laplacian pyramid: octave levels built by blurring and subsampling by two, storing band-pass residuals
primitives.verbatim_quote:
The best known (and probably most widely used) pyramid in computer vision is Burt
and Adelson’s (1983a) Laplacian pyramid. To construct the pyramid, we first blur and sub-
sample the original image by a factor of two and store this in the next level of the pyramid
assumptions: A sampling rate ratio of r = 2 between adjacent levels (an octave pyramid)
The blur kernel before subsampling is chosen to limit aliasing
primitives.breakdown_regime: Content that aliases under factor-two decimation is lost or folded into lower bands; the pyramid is redundant (overcomplete), so storage exceeds the original image

layer2.mapping: A coarse-to-fine stack where each level stores only what the level below cannot explain is the template for multi-resolution reasoning: solve the coarse version first, then let each finer level work only on the residual
layer2.telemetry: residual magnitude per scale level, coarse-level solution confidence

primitives.name: Bilateral filter: weights are the product of a Gaussian domain kernel and a data-dependent range kernel, giving edge-preserving smoothing
primitives.verbatim_quote:
range kernel measures appearance (intensity) similarity
to the center pixel, and the bilateral filter kernel is a product of these two.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.w(i,j,k,l): weight of neighbor (k,l) when filtering pixel (i,j), dimensionless

assumptions: Spatially close pixels are likely related (domain term)
Pixels with similar values are likely from the same surface, so dissimilar neighbors across an edge are downweighted (range term)
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails on shot noise spikes sitting at the center pixel and can halo near very strong edges; range scale mis-set either blurs edges or leaves noise

layer2.mapping: Weighting each piece of evidence by both proximity and similarity to the query value, multiplicatively, is a general robust-averaging kernel: the engine adopts it whenever a local estimate must resist contamination from a neighboring but different regime
layer2.telemetry: spatial and value distances per evidence item, effective sample size after weighting

primitives.name: Auto-correlation (structure tensor) matrix A from smoothed outer products of image gradients; its eigen-structure classifies corners, edges, and flat regions
primitives.verbatim_quote:
This matrix can be interpreted as a tensor (multiband) image, where the outer
products of the gradients ∇I are convolved with a weighting function w to provide a per-pixel
estimate of the local (quadratic) shape of the auto-correlation function.
primitives.latex: A = w \ast \begin{bmatrix} I_x^2 & I_x I_y \\ I_x I_y & I_y^2 \end{bmatrix}

symbol_and_unit_ledger.I_x, I_y: horizontal and vertical image derivatives, intensity per pixel

assumptions: A first-order Taylor expansion of the image function approximates the auto-correlation surface near zero shift
The weighting window is large enough to average gradient noise but small enough to stay local
primitives.breakdown_regime: The one-dimensional aperture problem: along a straight edge only the normal gradient component is observable, so one eigenvalue vanishes and localization along the edge is impossible

layer2.mapping: A local second-moment matrix whose eigenvalues separate well-constrained, partially constrained, and unconstrained directions is exactly an identifiability diagnostic; the engine reads eigenvalue ratios of local evidence curvature the same way to decide which directions of a question a data patch can answer
layer2.telemetry: eigenvalue pairs of local evidence curvature, aperture-like one-dimensional cases flagged

primitives.name: SIFT descriptor: Gaussian-weighted gradient orientation histograms over a 16x16 keypoint window, 128 values, unit-normalized and clipped at 0.2
primitives.verbatim_quote:
Scale invariant feature transform (SIFT). SIFT features are formed by computing the
gradient at each pixel in a 16×16 window around the detected keypoint, using the appropriate
level of the Gaussian pyramid at which the keypoint was detected.
assumptions: Keypoints are detected at a characteristic scale in the Gaussian pyramid, and gradients are sampled from that level
Soft (trilinear) assignment of gradient magnitudes to histogram bins reduces sensitivity to small misregistrations
primitives.breakdown_regime: Descriptors degrade under strong non-planar viewpoint change, motion blur, and in textureless regions where no stable keypoint exists

layer2.mapping: A fixed-length, normalized histogram of local orientation evidence, made invariant by construction and robustified by clipping, is the template for turning a messy local pattern into a comparable fingerprint; the engine uses the same recipe when it fingerprints recurring situations for retrieval
layer2.telemetry: descriptor vectors per situation, nearest-neighbor match distances and ratios

primitives.name: Hysteresis thresholding: two thresholds, a tracked contour may dip from the high threshold down to the low one without breaking
primitives.verbatim_quote:
hysteresis is to set two different thresholds and allow a curve being tracked above the higher
threshold to dip in strength down to the lower threshold.
assumptions: True contours have segments above the high threshold somewhere along their length
Noise rarely forms connected chains above the high threshold
primitives.breakdown_regime: A true contour that never reaches the high threshold is lost entirely; a noise chain touching a strong contour is absorbed into it

layer2.mapping: Dual thresholds with connectivity-based rescue is a general decision rule: strong evidence admits an item outright, weak evidence admits it only when connected to strong evidence; the engine uses it to keep faint but corroborated signals without opening the gate to isolated noise
layer2.telemetry: high and low threshold settings, counts of rescued versus isolated weak items

primitives.name: Hough transform: each edge point votes for all parameter values consistent with it; peaks in the accumulator are the detected structures
primitives.verbatim_quote:
The Hough transform, named after its original inventor (Hough 1962), is a well-known
technique for having edges “vote” for plausible line locations (Duda and Hart 1972; Ballard
1981; Illingworth and Kittler 1988). In its original formulation (Figure 4.41), each edge point
votes for all possible lines passing through it, and lines corresponding to high accumulator or
bin values are examined for potential line fits.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.r: signed perpendicular distance of the line from the origin, in pixels
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\theta: angle of the line normal, in radians or degrees

assumptions: The structure sought has a low-dimensional parameterization (here a line)
Enough collinear points exist that their votes coincide in one accumulator cell
primitives.breakdown_regime: Accumulator size explodes with parameter dimension; spurious peaks arise from structured clutter, and quantization trades resolution against vote splitting

layer2.mapping: Voting turns many weak, ambiguous local observations into a few strong global hypotheses by accumulating consistency in parameter space; the engine uses accumulator thinking whenever many partial signals each constrain a shared hypothesis
layer2.telemetry: vote counts per hypothesis cell, peak sharpness versus background votes

primitives.name: Snakes: an energy-minimizing 2D spline curve with internal continuity energy that evolves toward image features such as strong edges
primitives.verbatim_quote:
is an energy-minimizing, two-dimensional spline curve that evolves (moves)
towards image features such as strong edges.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.E_{int}: internal spline energy of the curve
symbol_and_unit_ledger.f(s) = (x(s), y(s)): curve position at arc length s
symbol_and_unit_ledger.f_s, f_{ss}: first and second derivatives along the curve

assumptions: The desired boundary is a smooth curve, so first and second derivative penalties are appropriate priors
An initialization reasonably close to the boundary is available
primitives.breakdown_regime: Local minima trap the curve when initialization is far from the boundary; sharp corners fight the rigidity term, and topology changes (splitting, merging) are not representable

layer2.mapping: Fitting by minimizing a sum of internal-consistency energy and external-evidence energy, with explicit smoothness weights, is the engine's generic shape for boundary and state estimation: the weights, not the data alone, decide how much wiggliness the answer is allowed
layer2.telemetry: energy decomposition per fit (internal versus external terms), initialization distance

primitives.name: Mean shift: non-parametric density modeling by kernel smoothing; segmentation by finding modes (peaks) and grouping points that climb to the same peak
primitives.verbatim_quote:
The key to mean shift is a technique for efficiently find-
ing peaks in this high-dimensional data distribution without ever computing the complete
function explicitly (Fukunaga and Hostetler 1975; Cheng 1995; Comaniciu and Meer 2002).

symbol_and_unit_ledger.f(x): kernel density estimate at point x
symbol_and_unit_ledger.h: kernel bandwidth (smoothing width), in data units

assumptions: Samples are drawn from an underlying density whose modes correspond to the segments sought
A single bandwidth h is appropriate across the feature space
primitives.breakdown_regime: Bandwidth choice dominates the result: too small fragments clusters, too large merges them; sparse high-dimensional data makes density peaks unreliable

layer2.mapping: Mode-seeking on a smoothed empirical density groups observations by the peak they climb to rather than by a prespecified cluster count; the engine uses this when the number of regimes in a data stream is unknown and must be discovered from the data itself
layer2.telemetry: bandwidth used, number and mass of modes found, points assigned per mode

primitives.name: Normalized cut: partition a pixel affinity graph by cut weight normalized by total association, avoiding degenerate single-pixel cuts
primitives.verbatim_quote:
While bottom-up merging techniques aggregate regions into coherent wholes and mean-shift
techniques try to find clusters of similar pixels using mode finding, the normalized cuts
technique introduced by Shi and Malik (2000) examines the affinities (similarities) between
nearby pixels and tries to separate groups that are connected by weak affinities.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.cut(A, B): sum of affinity weights w_ij over edges between groups A and B
symbol_and_unit_ledger.assoc(A, V): sum of all weights from nodes in A to all nodes V in the graph
symbol_and_unit_ledger.w_ij: similarity (affinity) between pixels or regions i and j, dimensionless

assumptions: Pairwise affinities between nearby pixels capture perceptual grouping
A balanced partition is preferred, which the association normalization enforces
primitives.breakdown_regime: Plain minimum cut degenerates to isolating single pixels, which is why the normalization exists; exact Ncut minimization is NP-hard, so the spectral relaxation can misplace boundaries

layer2.mapping: Normalizing a separation score by the total association of each side prevents trivial splits that isolate one element; the engine applies the same normalization whenever it scores how distinct two clusters of evidence are, so a lone outlier cannot fake a regime change
layer2.telemetry: cut weight and association totals per candidate partition, balance of resulting groups

primitives.name: MRF energy minimization (data term plus smoothness term) reformulated as max-flow/min-cut, with a guaranteed global minimum for submodular binary energies
primitives.verbatim_quote:
For simple energy functions, e.g., those where the penalty
for non-identical neighboring pixels is a constant, this algorithm is guaranteed to produce the
global minimum.
primitives.latex: E_d(i, j) = w(i, j)\,\rho_d\bigl(f(i, j) - d(i, j)\bigr)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\rho_d: robust penalty function on the data residual

assumptions: The energy's pairwise terms satisfy the regularity (submodularity) conditions of Kolmogorov and Zabih for exact graph-cut optimization
Neighboring pixels are expected to agree unless the data says otherwise (smoothness prior)
primitives.breakdown_regime: Non-submodular energies lose the global-minimum guarantee; multi-label problems need move-making approximations such as alpha-expansion, and simulated annealing performs notably worse

layer2.mapping: Writing an estimation problem as an explicit energy with a data term and a smoothness term, then solving it to a certified global optimum when the terms are submodular, is the engine's standard for structured decisions: the objective is auditable and the solver's guarantee is known before the answer is trusted
layer2.telemetry: energy values per candidate solution, submodularity checks on pairwise terms, optimality certificates

primitives.name: RANSAC: random minimal samples, inlier counting, and the trial count S = log(1-P)/log(1-p^k) needed for success probability P
primitives.verbatim_quote:
To ensure that the random sampling has a good chance of finding a true set of inliers, a
sufficient number of trials S must be tried.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.S: required number of random sampling trials
symbol_and_unit_ledger.P: target total probability of at least one all-inlier sample
symbol_and_unit_ledger.p: probability that any given correspondence is valid (an inlier)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.k: number of points in each minimal sample

assumptions: Inlier status of sampled correspondences is independent across draws
A distance threshold (often around 1-3 pixels) defines inliers, and the inlier set supports a final least-squares refit
primitives.breakdown_regime: Trial count explodes as k grows or p shrinks (at k=3, p=0.5, S=35 for 99 percent success); structured outliers that agree with a wrong model can win the inlier count

layer2.mapping: Consensus from minimal random subsets, scored by how much of the data agrees, is the engine's robust-fitting pattern when a large fraction of inputs may be corrupt; the trial-count formula prices the search honestly from the assumed contamination rate
layer2.telemetry: inlier counts per hypothesis, assumed inlier ratio, trials run versus trials required

primitives.name: Closed-form 3D alignment: orthogonal Procrustes via SVD of the correlation matrix (R = U V^T), or Horn's quaternion eigenvector method
primitives.verbatim_quote:
Another technique is the absolute orientation algorithm (Horn 1987) for estimating the
unit quaternion corresponding to the rotation matrix R, which involves forming a 4×4 matrix
from the entries in C and then finding the eigenvector associated with its largest positive
eigenvalue.
primitives.latex: C = \sum_i \hat{x}'_i \hat{x}_i^T = U\Sigma V^T, \qquad R = U V^T

symbol_and_unit_ledger.C: 3x3 correlation matrix of the centered point sets
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\hat{x}_i, \\hat{x}'_i: corresponding 3D points after subtracting their centroids
symbol_and_unit_ledger.U, \\Sigma, V: singular value decomposition factors of C
symbol_and_unit_ledger.R: optimal rotation matrix in the least-squares sense

assumptions: Correspondences between the two point sets are known
Centroid subtraction decouples translation from rotation; the noise model is isotropic for the plain closed form
primitives.breakdown_regime: Wrong correspondences or anisotropic, per-point covariances break the closed form and require iterative optimization; a reflection (det R = -1) must be explicitly excluded

layer2.mapping: When two views of the same underlying objects must be registered, the least-squares optimal rigid alignment has a closed form; the engine uses this pattern to align evidence frames before differencing them, instead of comparing unregistered quantities
layer2.telemetry: correspondence lists, centroid offsets, alignment residuals after registration

primitives.name: Pose estimation (extrinsic calibration, PnP): recover a camera's 3D pose from 2D projections of known 3D points, minimally the P3P problem
primitives.verbatim_quote:
A particular instance of feature-based alignment, which occurs very often, is estimating an
object’s 3D pose from a set of 2D point projections. This pose estimation problem is also
known as extrinsic calibration,
assumptions: The 3D coordinates of the reference points and their 2D image projections are known
Camera intrinsics are either known or recovered jointly (the DLT recovers a full 3x4 camera matrix)
primitives.breakdown_regime: The minimal three-point problem has up to four solutions needing disambiguation; planar or collinear point configurations are degenerate, and noisy points favor iterative statistically optimal refinements over the linear DLT

layer2.mapping: Recovering the observer's own position from the projections of known landmarks is the template for self-location inside any observation frame: the engine treats its own vantage (which data window, which era, which source mix) as an estimable pose rather than a given
layer2.telemetry: landmark correspondences used, reprojection residuals, pose covariance

primitives.name: Triangulation: a point's 3D position from corresponding image locations and known camera positions, the converse of pose estimation
primitives.verbatim_quote:
The problem of determining a point’s 3D position from a set of corresponding image locations
and known camera positions is known as triangulation.
assumptions: Camera positions and calibration are known
Corresponding image locations refer to the same physical point
primitives.breakdown_regime: Small baseline angles make depth ill-conditioned (rays nearly parallel); mismatched correspondences place the point at a phantom location nearest to inconsistent rays

layer2.mapping: Intersecting independent lines of sight to localize a hidden quantity, with uncertainty governed by the angle between the views, is the engine's model for combining independent evidence channels about one latent variable
layer2.telemetry: viewing angles between evidence channels, localization uncertainty per estimate

primitives.name: Epipolar constraint: corresponding normalized image points satisfy x1^T E x0 = 0 with essential matrix E = [t]x R
primitives.verbatim_quote: We therefore arrive at the basic epipolar constraint

symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\hat{x}_0, \\hat{x}_1: normalized (calibration-corrected) image coordinates of the same 3D point in two views
symbol_and_unit_ledger.E: essential matrix encoding relative camera pose
symbol_and_unit_ledger.[t]_\\times: skew-symmetric cross-product matrix of the translation vector t
symbol_and_unit_ledger.R: relative rotation between the two cameras

assumptions: Cameras are calibrated so pixel measurements can be converted to normalized ray directions
The scene point is static between the two views
primitives.breakdown_regime: Pure rotation (zero translation) makes E vanish; planar scenes and critical surfaces give ambiguous solutions, and uncalibrated cameras need the fundamental matrix instead

layer2.mapping: A bilinear constraint that two observations of the same hidden point must satisfy, parameterized by a small set of relative-pose unknowns, lets the engine test consistency of paired evidence and solve for the relationship between the observers at the same time
layer2.telemetry: residuals of the constraint per pair, estimated relative pose, degenerate-motion flags

primitives.name: Factorization (Tomasi-Kanade): under orthography the measurement matrix factors as motion times structure, recovered by rank-3 SVD
primitives.verbatim_quote:
structure and motion can simultaneously be estimated using factorization (singular value de-
composition), as discussed in Section 7.3 (Tomasi and Kanade 1992).

symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\hat{X}: measurement matrix of tracked point coordinates across frames
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\hat{M}: motion matrix, 2M x 3 for M frames, built from camera rotation rows
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\hat{S}: structure matrix, 3 x N for N points, the 3D point coordinates
symbol_and_unit_ledger.rank 3: the noiseless measurement matrix has exactly three nonzero singular values under orthography

assumptions: Orthographic (or scaled orthographic) projection, so projection is linear in the 3D points
All points are tracked through all frames (complete measurement matrix)
primitives.breakdown_regime: Perspective effects, missing tracks, and independently moving objects violate the single rank-3 model; the SVD factorization is only recovered up to a 3x3 ambiguity matrix Q that metric constraints must fix

layer2.mapping: A large observation matrix that factors into an observer part and a world part, with the rank revealing the latent dimension, is the engine's template for separating how things were measured from what was measured
layer2.telemetry: singular value spectra of evidence matrices, completeness of the observation grid

primitives.name: Bundle adjustment: simultaneous non-linear least squares over all camera and 3D structure parameters minimizing reprojection error; the standard method for structure from motion
primitives.verbatim_quote:
Bundle adjustment is now the standard method of choice for most structure-from-motion
problems and is commonly applied to problems with hundreds of weakly calibrated images
and tens of thousands of points, e.g., in systems such as Photosynth.
assumptions: A good initialization exists (for example from factorization or incremental registration)
Measurement noise is roughly Gaussian, or a robust loss replaces the plain squares
primitives.breakdown_regime: Scale grows cubically in a naive solve, so very large problems need sparse or incremental variants; gauge freedoms (global scale, coordinate frame) make the Hessian rank-deficient unless fixed

layer2.mapping: Jointly refining every parameter of a coupled system against all observations, rather than freezing early estimates, is the engine's endgame pattern for any multi-part model: local estimates initialize, then one global reconciliation pass owns the final numbers
layer2.telemetry: reprojection-style residuals per observation, parameter counts, sparsity pattern of the joint system

primitives.name: Brightness constancy (optical flow constraint) equation: Ix u + Iy v + It = 0, one equation per pixel for two unknown flow components
primitives.verbatim_quote:
The linearized form of the incremental update to the SSD error (8.35) is often called the
optical flow constraint or brightness constancy constraint equation

symbol_and_unit_ledger.I_x, I_y: spatial image derivatives, intensity per pixel
symbol_and_unit_ledger.I_t: temporal image derivative, intensity per frame
symbol_and_unit_ledger.u, v: horizontal and vertical components of the optical flow (image velocity), pixels per frame

assumptions: A point's brightness stays constant as it moves between frames
Motion is small enough that the first-order Taylor linearization holds
primitives.breakdown_regime: The aperture problem: one equation cannot determine two unknowns, so only the flow component along the gradient is observable locally; illumination changes and occlusions violate constancy outright

layer2.mapping: A conservation assumption linearized into one constraint per observation tells the engine exactly which component of change is measurable and which is invisible (the aperture direction); unobservable components must be filled by priors, never by pretending the data spoke
layer2.telemetry: per-observation constraint residuals, fraction of change lying in the unobservable direction

primitives.name: Camera response recovery and HDR assembly: multiple bracketed exposures of a static scene jointly estimate per-pixel irradiance and the camera response curve
primitives.verbatim_quote:
The easiest approach is probably to take multiple exposures of the same scene while the
camera is on a tripod and to recover the response function by simultaneously estimating the
incoming irradiance at each pixel and the response curve (Mann and Picard 1995; Debevec
assumptions: The scene and camera are static across exposures (tripod), so only exposure time varies
The response function is the same for all pixels and monotonic
primitives.breakdown_regime: Scene motion between exposures ghosts the merged result; clipped (saturated or black) pixels in all exposures carry no irradiance information

layer2.mapping: Recovering an unknown sensor response by observing the same quantity at several known gains, then inverting it to extend dynamic range, is the engine's calibration pattern for any source whose reporting scale is non-linear or clipped
layer2.telemetry: response curve estimates per source, fraction of observations clipped at each gain

primitives.name: Super-resolution: align and combine several low-resolution input images (modeled through the stochastic image formation equations) into a higher-resolution composite
primitives.verbatim_quote:
super-resolution refers to the process of aligning and combining several input images
to produce such high-resolution composites (Irani and Peleg 1991; Cheeseman, Kanefsky,
assumptions: Sub-pixel relative motion between the input frames provides the complementary samples
The blur and downsampling formation model is known or estimable, and priors regularize the ill-posed inversion
primitives.breakdown_regime: Integer-pixel-aligned inputs add no new samples; aliasing beyond the sensor limit and wrong motion estimates turn reconstruction into hallucination

layer2.mapping: Many individually insufficient observations, each shifted by a known sub-unit offset, jointly determine a finer quantity than any single observation; the engine uses this whenever repeated noisy measurements with known offsets can be fused instead of averaged
layer2.telemetry: relative offsets between observations, fused resolution gain, per-observation blur estimates

primitives.name: Stereo disparity: under fronto-parallel imaging, horizontal disparity between two views is inversely proportional to scene distance
primitives.verbatim_quote:
As we will shortly see, under simple imaging configurations (both eyes or cameras look-
ing straight ahead), the amount of horizontal motion or disparity is inversely proportional to
the distance from the observer.
assumptions: Both cameras look straight ahead with parallel optical axes (rectified geometry)
Correspondences between the two images can be established densely and accurately
primitives.breakdown_regime: Textureless, occluded, or specular regions defeat correspondence; disparity resolution limits make distant depth differences unmeasurable, which is why inverse depth is the better-conditioned parameterization

layer2.mapping: A quantity that enters through its reciprocal is better estimated and stored as the reciprocal; the engine adopts inverse (disparity-like) parameterizations whenever the direct quantity compresses all distant distinctions into numerical noise
layer2.telemetry: disparity-style measurements per item, depth uncertainty growth with distance

primitives.name: Shape from shading: recover surface shape from intensity variation through the reflectance map I(x,y) = R(p,q) relating brightness to surface orientation
primitives.verbatim_quote:
The problem of recovering the shape of a surface from this intensity variation is known as
shape from shading and is one of the classic problems in computer vision (Horn 1975).
primitives.latex: I(x, y) = R(p(x, y), q(x, y))

symbol_and_unit_ledger.I(x, y): measured image irradiance at pixel (x, y)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.R: reflectance map, brightness as a function of surface orientation
symbol_and_unit_ledger.p = z_x, q = z_y: partial derivatives of the depth map z(x, y), dimensionless slopes

assumptions: Uniform albedo and reflectance across the surface
Light source directions are known or calibratable with a reference object, and sources and observer are distant
primitives.breakdown_regime: One brightness value per pixel cannot by itself fix two orientation unknowns (bas-relief ambiguity); albedo changes masquerade as shape changes

layer2.mapping: Inverting a known forward map from hidden orientation-like variables to a scalar observation is underdetermined pointwise and only closes with integrability and boundary constraints; the engine treats such single-channel inversions as constraint generators, not as direct measurements
layer2.telemetry: per-point constraint residuals, integrability violations of the recovered field

primitives.name: Plenoptic function and light field: scene appearance as a 5D function of camera position and ray direction, reducible to 4D in free space
primitives.verbatim_quote:
Thus, taking the cross-product of the three-dimensional space of camera positions with the
2D space of spherical images, we obtain the 5D plenoptic function of Adelson and Bergen
assumptions: The scene is static: objects and illuminants fixed, only the observer moves
No participating media (smoke or fog), so coincident rays along free space share one color, allowing the 5D to 4D reduction
primitives.breakdown_regime: Dynamic scenes, view-dependent effects needing the full ray parameterization, and sparse sampling all break the representation; capture density grows explosively with viewpoint coverage

layer2.mapping: Tabulating a phenomenon as a function over the full space of viewpoints, then exploiting redundancy (free-space constancy) to compress it, is the engine's model for precomputed evidence stores: enumerate the viewpoint space once, answer new queries by interpolation
layer2.telemetry: viewpoint coverage of stored evidence, interpolation distances for new queries

primitives.name: Visual words: cluster high-dimensional feature descriptors (k-means on SIFT) into a discrete vocabulary so images become word histograms searchable with inverted indices
primitives.verbatim_quote:
In order to apply fast information retrieval techniques to images, the high-dimensional
feature descriptors that occur in each image must first be mapped into discrete visual words.
assumptions: A clustering of descriptors learned from a sample of frames generalizes to new images
Very common words behave like stop words and are dropped so they do not contaminate matching
primitives.breakdown_regime: Quantization discards descriptor detail, so visually different patches collide in one word; vocabulary size trades recall against index size and clustering cost

layer2.mapping: Discretizing continuous evidence into a learned vocabulary of recurring patterns converts comparison into counting, enabling inverted-index retrieval over huge archives; the engine uses word-style histograms whenever it must search many stored situations for ones resembling a query
layer2.telemetry: vocabulary size, word histograms per stored item, stop-word rates, retrieval ranks

reasoning_traces.think: This book is a complete working map of classical computer vision, organized as a pipeline that runs from how images are formed to how they are interpreted, and its deepest lesson is that every stage is an inverse problem with a specific, nameable ambiguity. Chapter 2 builds the forward model: homogeneous coordinates and projective geometry describe projection, perspective division destroys depth, Lambertian reflection ties brightness to surface orientation, and the Bayer array shows that even the sensor is a designed compromise that samples green twice as densely as red or blue because luminance carries the detail. If the forward model is understood, the rest of the book is a catalog of inversions, each with its own failure mode written next to it. Chapter 3 supplies the linear machinery: convolution as the general linear shift-invariant operator, the Fourier transform as its frequency portrait, pyramids for coarse-to-fine work, and the bilateral filter as the first place where the book deliberately breaks linearity so that edges survive smoothing. Chapter 4 turns images into discrete, matchable evidence: the structure tensor reads local identifiability off its eigenvalues, SIFT packages a patch into a normalized orientation histogram that can be compared across viewpoints, hysteresis thresholding admits weak evidence only when it is connected to strong evidence, and the Hough transform converts scattered local votes into global hypotheses. Chapter 5 groups pixels into regions with three different philosophies that recur everywhere in the book: deform a curve under an energy (snakes), climb a smoothed density to its modes (mean shift), or cut a graph under a normalized criterion (normalized cuts), with graph cuts returning in Chapter 3 and throughout as the workhorse that minimizes explicit data-plus-smoothness energies to a certified optimum when the terms are submodular. Chapters 6 and 7 are the geometric core, and they read as one long argument about estimation under contamination and coupling. Robust fitting starts with RANSAC, whose trial-count formula prices random search from the inlier ratio and the sample size, and continues through closed-form alignment (Procrustes and absolute orientation), pose estimation from point correspondences, triangulation as the converse problem, and the epipolar constraint as a bilinear consistency test between two views. Factorization shows the elegant linear special case in which the whole measurement matrix splits into motion times structure by rank-3 SVD, and bundle adjustment then gives the general answer: throw away the closed forms and jointly refine every camera and point against every observation, accepting a sparse non-linear least squares problem as the price of correctness. Chapter 8 repeats the pattern for motion, where brightness constancy yields one equation for two unknowns and the aperture problem states precisely which component of the truth the data cannot see. Chapters 9 through 13 apply the machinery: stitching registers images with homographies and global alignment, computational photography inverts the sensor itself (recovering response curves from bracketed exposures and fusing offset low-resolution frames into super-resolution), stereo turns disparity into depth with an inverse relationship that argues for inverse-depth parameterizations, shape from shading inverts a reflectance map under an integrability constraint, and the light field chapter tabulates appearance over the whole viewpoint space and compresses it by a free-space redundancy argument. Chapter 14 closes the loop to recognition by quantizing descriptors into visual words, which converts image search into text-style retrieval with inverted indices. For a reasoning engine, the transferable content is not any single algorithm but the discipline the book applies uniformly: write the forward model, name the ambiguity it creates, choose an estimator whose guarantee matches the contamination and coupling of the problem, and keep the decomposition of every objective visible (data term versus prior term, observable versus unobservable components, per-scale residuals). An engine that borrows this discipline can say, for each of its estimates, which part came from measurement, which part came from a prior, which directions were never observable, and what additional independent view would most reduce the remaining uncertainty. Where the book breaks is equally instructive: nearly every method assumes a static, Lambertian, well-textured world observed by a calibrated pinhole camera, and the text is honest that real scenes violate all four, which is why its later chapters lean increasingly on global optimization and learned statistics rather than pure geometry. A second thread worth extracting is the book's treatment of optimization as a design choice with known guarantees rather than a black box. Simulated annealing is presented and then honestly demoted: the comparative evaluation work the author led (Szeliski, Zabih, Scharstein et al. 2008) benchmarks stereo and MRF solvers against each other, and the text repeatedly tells the reader which solver family wins on which energy class, graph cuts for submodular binary and ordinal problems, belief propagation and dynamic programming where structure allows, gradient methods where the energy is smooth. That benchmarking habit, reporting that a popular technique does not perform that well and showing the comparison, is itself a primitive: claims about estimators are settled by controlled comparison on shared data, not by the elegance of the derivation. A third thread is the deliberate alternation between feature-based and direct methods. Feature-based pipelines compress images into sparse, robust, matchable tokens and then do clean geometry on the tokens, at the cost of discarding most of the pixels; direct methods use every pixel through brightness constancy and SSD energies, at the cost of small-motion linearizations and sensitivity to illumination. The book teaches the reader to choose based on baseline, texture, and expected deformation, and to hybridize: features to initialize and to reject outliers, direct refinement to finish. A fourth thread is uncertainty. The structure tensor's inverse bounds localization uncertainty, RANSAC's inlier threshold is an explicit noise model, bundle adjustment carries covariances through its normal equations, and the exercises return to calibration accuracy again and again. Estimates in this book are expected to arrive with a statement of how wrong they might be and in which direction, which is the habit that separates a measurement from a guess. Finally, the recognition chapter marks the field's turn from geometry to statistics: once descriptors exist, clustering them into visual words and counting words per image imports the whole machinery of text retrieval, and the frontier problems become dataset design, evaluation protocol, and learning the priors that the earlier chapters wrote down by hand.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The lineage runs from photogrammetry and radiometry through Marr's computational theory of vision to the estimation-theoretic synthesis of the 1980s and 1990s: Harris and Stephens on corners (1988), Kass, Witkin, and Terzopoulos on snakes (1988), Tomasi and Kanade on factorization (1992), and Lowe on SIFT (2004). Szeliski writes from inside the Microsoft Research and Digital Equipment Corporation laboratory tradition, and the book's seeds were a 2001 University of Washington course co-taught with Steve Seitz on computer vision for computer graphics, which explains its constant pull toward applications that must work on real photographs.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: The author models the reader as a builder: a senior undergraduate or graduate student who will implement each algorithm and discover its failure modes personally through the exercises. His stated editorial rule is to emphasize basic techniques that work under real-world conditions over mathematically elegant but impractical ones, and he assumes the reader accepts that vision is an inverse problem, so every method is presented together with the ambiguity it cannot resolve and the prior it uses to resolve the rest.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: Several results in this book veto naive designs in any layered inference system. The aperture problem vetoes any claim that a local measurement determines a full vector quantity: only the component along the gradient exists in the data. Perspective projection vetoes depth claims from a single view, and the RANSAC trial formula vetoes robust fitting attempted with too few samples for the assumed outlier rate. The submodularity conditions veto guaranteed global optimization for arbitrary energies, and the plain minimum cut's degeneracy vetoes unnormalized separation scores anywhere they are used.

universal_lens: The book is a general template for inverting any sensing process: model the forward map honestly, enumerate exactly what information it destroys, and then design estimators whose priors repair precisely that destruction and no more. Its recurring moves, multiscale residuals, voting in parameter space, energy decomposition into data and prior terms, and joint refinement of coupled unknowns, transfer to any domain where observations are indirect, noisy, and incomplete.
gsi_mapping: For the Institute, this work supplies the measurement-science core of the curriculum: projective geometry, photometric image formation, frequency analysis, and estimation theory presented as one connected story with named failure regimes. Its exercise-driven structure, in which students implement each method and watch it break on real photographs, is the model for teaching inference as a craft of forward models and ambiguity budgets rather than as a catalog of algorithms.
gse_mapping: For the Edge engine, the book contributes its estimation discipline rather than any vision algorithm: observable-versus-unobservable decomposition from the aperture problem, consensus fitting with an honestly priced trial budget from RANSAC, joint global refinement in the style of bundle adjustment, and explicit data-term versus prior-term accounting in every objective. Its camera and broadcast geometry also grounds the engine's video analysis surfaces, where homographies, triangulation, and motion estimation operate on game footage.
